name: bluewater-24-echigoya
lines: In sixteen seventy three, a fifty two year old man opened a cloth shop in Japan.
Within ten years, the other merchants had forced him off his street.
His crime? He put prices on things.
That shop is still open today. And his family name is on one of the biggest companies in Japan.
This is how one shop broke every rule of selling. And why every rule he broke still works.
First, the old way. In Edo, the city we now call Tokyo, fine cloth is sold to the rich.
The seller comes to your house. With his finest rolls. And a smile.
There is no price. There is a conversation.
What you pay depends on who you are, and how well you argue.
You buy the whole roll. And you pay later, on credit, months from now.
It works beautifully, if you're rich. Everyone else is not invited.
Then comes Mitsui Takatoshi. He is not a young man with a new idea. He is fifty two.
He opens his shop, and calls it Echigoya.
And he looks at all the people the other shops ignore.
Ordinary townspeople. With a little money. And nobody selling to them.
So he breaks the first rule. He stops going to houses. You come to the shop.
Rule two. No credit. You pay cash, today.
Rule three. And this is the big one. One price. For everybody.
Written down. No arguing. A servant pays what a lord pays.
Rule four. You don't have to buy the whole roll. He'll cut any length you want.
Need a robe in a hurry? He has tailors right there in the shop.
Fair prices. Small orders. Fast work. For anyone who walks in.
The shop fills up. And the other merchants are furious.
In sixteen eighty three, their anger forces him to move the whole shop.
Most people would go quiet after that. He does the opposite.
He prints flyers. The first that city has ever seen. And he sends them all over Edo.
They say exactly what he does. Cash only. Prices as marked.
He is not hiding the thing they hated him for. He is advertising it.
And then, the move I love most. It starts to rain.
Customers are stuck in his shop, with no way home.
So the shop lends them umbrellas. Free.
Each one has the shop's mark painted on it. Big.
Now picture the city in a storm. People everywhere. All carrying his name.
It wasn't an ad. It was a favour. That's why it worked.
The shop grew into one of the largest stores in Japan.
Today it's a department store called Mitsukoshi. Still on that same spot.
And the family became Mitsui.
So here's what a cloth seller from the sixteen hundreds can teach you.
One. Say your price. People trust what they can see.
Two. Serve the customer everyone else thinks is too small.
Three. Make it easy. Any size job. Fast. No games.
Four. Tell the whole town exactly what you do.
And five. Put your name on something useful, and give it away.
Three hundred and fifty years later, it still works. Because people haven't changed.
Your business. Our marketing department. Bluewater Co.
